paragraphs.text: Osteogenesis imperfecta type XIII is an autosomal recessive bone fragility disorder caused by deficient activity of the procollagen I C-terminal propeptide endopeptidase BMP1. Reported patients have had recurrent fractures, which in some started at or before birth. Some also had bone deformities, short stature, and umbilical hernia (Martinez-Glez et al., 2012; Cho et al., 2015). Bone density has varied between reports. It was described as low in the original Egyptian sibs (Martinez-Glez et al., 2012) but as increased or normal in other patients (Asharani et al., 2012; Valencia et al., 2014; Fahiminiya et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Munns et al. (2004) described 3 unrelated children with an apparently novel bone fragility disorder associated with an idiopathic mineralization defect. Recurrent lower limb fractures started when the children began bearing weight. The patients had none of the phenotypic, radiologic, or histomorphometric features classically associated with OI, idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis, or mild autosomal dominant osteopetrosis. Radiographs showed increased metaphyseal trabeculation and normal to increased cortical thickness, with no evidence of rickets or osteomalacia. Areal and volumetric bone mineral density (BMD) of the lumbar spine showed no major alteration. In 1 patient, peripheral quantitative computed tomography (pQCT) of the radius showed elevated cortical thickness and elevated total and trabecular volumetric BMD. Iliac bone biopsies showed a paucity of the birefringent pattern of normal lamellar bone. Histomorphometry showed osteomalacia with a prolonged mineralization lag time and a decreased mineral apposition rate. There was no biochemical evidence of abnormal calcium or phosphate metabolism, and mutation analysis of type I collagen was negative. Munns et al. (2004) concluded that this was a bone fragility disorder of moderate severity associated with accumulation of osteoid due to an intrinsic mineralization defect.

paragraphs.text: Martinez-Glez et al. (2012) studied 2 sibs with severe autosomal recessive OI from a consanguineous Egyptian family. Their parents were first cousins. The proband was a 15-year-old girl. A fracture of the left tibia was noted after a normal full-term vaginal delivery, and she subsequently had 10 to 15 spontaneous fractures per year in the upper and lower limbs. Her features included triangular face, broad forehead, wide palpebral fissures, long eyelashes, faint blue sclerae, long philtrum, thin lips, and prominent ears. Her gross motor development was delayed and she could not stand unsupported. Mental development was normal, and she had no dentinogenesis imperfecta. She had a relatively large thorax compressing the abdomen and a large umbilical hernia (5 cm wide and 7 cm long) with abdominal contents. Other features included generalized hypotonia, muscle wasting, nocturnal enuresis, and generalized hirsutism. Her skin stretched normally, with no bruising or scars. Severe generalized bone deformities were painful to touch and included deformed clavicles, bowed and angulated upper limb bones, bowed femora, and severely angulated leg bones. She also had arachnodactyly, hyperextensibility of the elbow, wrist, and interphalangeal joints, kyphoscoliosis, and pectus carinatum. Radiographs showed deformed long bones with multiple fractures and callus formation, lack of bone modeling, serpentine thin tibiae and fibulae, S-curve thoracolumbar scoliosis with platyspondyly, generalized decreased bone density, and wormian bones. At 13 years of age, her weight was -3.8 SD, length -11.5 SD, and head circumference -3.0 SD. DEXA at 15 years showed borderline osteoporosis at the hip and spine (Z-scores -2.22 and -2.13, respectively).

paragraphs.text: The proband's 5-year-old brother had bilateral femoral bowing detected on fetal ultrasound and fractures of both femora at birth (Martinez-Glez et al., 2012). He had about 15 fractures per year. His facial features resembled his sister's, and like her he had normal mentality, no dentinogenesis imperfecta, and was unable to stand unsupported. He also had generalized bone deformities, joint hyperextensibility, arachnodactyly, and a large thorax with a large umbilical hernia (4 cm wide and 5 cm long). Radiographs showed wormian bones, deformed and unmodeled long bones with fractures, scoliosis, platyspondyly, and a wide symphysis pubis. His weight was -3.7 SD and length -7.2 SD, with normal head circumference. DEXA at 5 years showed borderline osteoporosis at the spine (Z-score -1.63) and osteoporosis at the left femur (Z-score -2.75). Audiologic and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable in both sibs. Serum calcium and phosphate were normal, and alkaline phosphatase was slightly high. Both sibs were diagnosed with OI type III according to the classification of Sillence et al. (1979). Martinez-Glez et al. (2012) noted that the patients did not have the increased skin stretchability and fragility seen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs from a consanguineous Egyptian family with severe autosomal recessive OI, Martinez-Glez et al. (2012) identified a homozygous missense mutation in the BMP1 gene (F249L). The mutation was found by sequencing BMP1, a candidate gene in a region identified by homozygosity mapping. It segregated with the disorder in the family. It was not found in 100 control chromosomes of the same ethnic origin or in 884 chromosomes from European controls. No mutations were found in COL1A1 or COL1A2 in 1 of the patients. Phe249 lies in the protease domain and is conserved in all members of the astacin family of metalloproteases. Supernatants from patient fibroblasts contained less pN-alpha-1(I) relative to pC-alpha-1(I) and less free C-propeptide (PICP) than controls, indicating reduced processing of the procollagen I C-propeptide. Fibroblasts from a heterozygous sib showed slightly impaired processing. Only wildtype mTLD improved processing in patient fibroblasts.

paragraphs.text: In a Korean patient with OI13, Cho et al. (2015) identified compound heterozygous variants in the BMP1 gene by whole-exome sequencing: a c.808A-G transition resulting in a met270-to-val (M270V) substitution, and a c.1297G-T change that caused skipping of exon 10. The patient had umbilical hernia, frequent fractures, markedly short stature, delayed motor development, scoliosis, and dislocation of the radial head. A zebrafish assay showed that both variants were hypofunctional.
